raw_case_text:
A 24-year-old female was brought to the emergency department with complaints of altered mental status and recurrent seizures associated with low-grade fever, headache, and altered sensorium for the last three days. The seizure was acute in onset, generalized tonic-clonic in nature, and associated with tongue biting, blood-tinged frothing, and urinary incontinence. It was her second episode of abnormal body movement and altered sensorium after being admitted to the hospital. Each episode lasted for 20-30 minutes. She returned from a hill station a few days ago, and her family and social history were insignificant.
On admission, the patient was afebrile, with a blood pressure of 110/70 mmHg, a Spo2 of 97%, and a heart rate of 86/min. Her physical examination revealed a Glasgow coma scale (GCS) score of 11 (eye: 4, verbal: 2, motor: 5). Her rest systemic examination was unremarkable. Her initial laboratory investigations were within normal range except for mild elevation of transaminases (Table 1). Further evaluation with a non-contrast computed tomography (CT) head shows a ring-enhancing lesion in the left temporal region with perifocal edema, an eccentric, and an inflammatory granuloma (Figure 1). In addition, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain showed a well-defined rounded discrete hyperintense lesion in the left parietal region with mild to moderate vasogenic edema, leading to partial effacement of the adjoining sub-arachnoid space and moderate peripheral rim enhancement (Figure 2). On follow-up after two weeks, an MR venogram revealed that the left transverse sinus was hypoplastic, as shown in Figure 3.
Following confirmation of diagnosis, the patient was started on albendazole 400mg twice daily and carbamazepine. However, on follow-up after two weeks, the patient developed skin rashes, remarkably elevated liver enzymes, and total bilirubin (Figure 4).
After proper evaluation, immediately anti-epileptic drugs were discontinued, and for skin rashes, the patient was given oral fexofenadine and methylprednisolone, levetiracetam beside topical steroids. On subsequent follow-up, her rashes and deranged aminases resolved, and the patient was doing well.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 24-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with a 3-day history of low-grade fever, headache, altered sensorium, and recurrent prolonged generalized tonic-clonic seizures.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the 3 days prior to admission, the patient developed low-grade fever, headache, depressed sensorium, and acute generalized tonic-clonic seizures lasting 20-30 minutes each, accompanied by tongue biting, blood-tinged oral frothing, and urinary incontinence, including a second prolonged episode after hospital admission.
subjective.past_medical_history: Returned from a trip to a hill station a few days prior to presentation; family and social histories were unremarkable.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for low-grade fever, headache, tongue biting, and urinary incontinence.

objective.physical_examination: On admission, she was afebrile with blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, heart rate 86/min, oxygen saturation 97%, and a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 11 (E4V2M5). The remainder of the systemic examination was unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial baseline laboratory tests were normal except for mildly elevated hepatic transaminases. At 2-week follow-up after starting albendazole and carbamazepine, repeat liver function tests showed markedly elevated transaminases and total bilirubin.
objective.advanced_workup: Noncontrast head CT revealed a ring-enhancing inflammatory granuloma with an eccentric nodule and perifocal edema in the left temporal region. Brain MRI demonstrated a well-defined rounded discrete hyperintense lesion in the left temporoparietal region with moderate peripheral rim enhancement, mild-to-moderate vasogenic edema, and partial effacement of the adjacent subarachnoid space. Two-week follow-up MR venography showed a hypoplastic left transverse sinus.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Parenchymal neurocysticercosis (inflammatory granuloma stage) was confirmed on neuroimaging, and the patient was initiated on oral albendazole 400 mg twice daily and carbamazepine. Two weeks later, she presented with drug-induced maculopapular skin rash and severe drug-induced liver injury (markedly elevated transaminases and hyperbilirubinemia); carbamazepine and albendazole were immediately discontinued and she was treated with levetiracetam, oral fexofenadine, oral methylprednisolone, and topical corticosteroids, achieving complete resolution of the rash and normalization of liver enzymes on subsequent follow-up.
